name: Gale Sayers
aliases: Gale Eugene Sayers; The Kansas Comet
description: Gale Sayers (May 30, 1943, Wichita, Kansas – September 23, 2020) — the 'Kansas Comet' — was the Chicago Bears halfback whose open-field running remains the standard for elusiveness in professional football. A two-time consensus All-American at Kansas, he was drafted fourth overall by the Bears in 1965 and set a league record with 22 touchdowns as a rookie, including a record-tying six in one game, while gaining 2,272 all-purpose yards. A severe right-knee injury cut short his 1968 season; he returned in 1969 to lead the NFL in rushing and win Comeback Player of the Year, before a second knee injury ended his career after seven seasons and only 68 games. His friendship with teammate Brian Piccolo, who died of cancer in 1970, produced his autobiography I Am Third and the film Brian's Song. In 1977, at thirty-four, he became the youngest person ever inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

name: Good Times
description: Good Times, created by Eric Monte and Mike Evans and developed by Norman Lear, aired on CBS from February 8, 1974, to August 1, 1979 — six seasons, 133 episodes following James and Florida Evans and their three children in a Chicago housing project, identified in coverage of the series as Cabrini-Green. It arrived through the Lear spin-off chain — All in the Family to Maude, whose housekeeper Florida Evans the series carried home — and it holds a first the shelf needs: it is cited as the first network television series built around a two-parent Black family, where earlier Black-led series such as Julia and Sanford and Son had centered single parents. The Evanses' subject was economics — James's patchwork of jobs, the rent, the children's futures — argued at a kitchen table in public housing on Chicago's Near North Side, in the city this graph calls home. 'Dy-no-mite' was the catchphrase; the record's claim is the setting: working-class Black Chicago, at the center of a hit network sitcom, in prime time, in 1974.

name: Gil Scott-Heron
description: Gil Scott-Heron (born April 1, 1949, in Chicago, Illinois; died May 27, 2011, in New York City) was an American poet, musician, and author whose spoken-word recordings fused poetry with jazz, soul, and blues into a new form of protest music. Born in Chicago and raised largely by his grandmother in Jackson, Tennessee, he attended Lincoln University in Pennsylvania and published his first book, The Vulture, in 1970. His debut album, Small Talk at 125th and Lenox (1970), carried “The Revolution Will Not Be Televised,” the satiric anthem that made him a defining voice of Black protest; Pieces of a Man (1971) and “Johannesburg” (1975) followed, made with his musical partner Brian Jackson. History calls him the godfather of rap — a title he rejected, preferring to call his work “bluesology.” He returned in 2010 with the acclaimed I'm New Here, received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2012, and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

description: Gladys Knight & the Pips were an Atlanta family vocal group formed in 1952 as the Pips by Gladys Knight, her brother Merald "Bubba" Knight, her sister Brenda Knight and their cousins William and Eleanor Guest, taking the name from cousin James "Pip" Woods. After Brenda Knight and Eleanor Guest left in 1959, cousin Edward Patten joined, and the settled lineup of Gladys Knight, Bubba Knight, Patten and William Guest lasted until the group disbanded in 1989. The group first hit with "Every Beat of My Heart" in 1961, signed with Motown Records in 1966 and recorded the first hit version of "I Heard It Through the Grapevine" in 1967. Moving to Buddah Records in 1973, they released the Grammy-winning number-one single "Midnight Train to Georgia" and the album Imagination. Later work included the Curtis Mayfield-produced Claudine soundtrack in 1974 and the Grammy-winning "Love Overboard" in 1987. The group won multiple Grammy Awards and was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1996, presented by Mariah Carey, and into the Vocal Group Hall of Fame in 2001.

name: George Cleveland Hall Branch Library
description: The first full-service Chicago Public Library branch in Bronzeville, opened January 18, 1932. Named for Dr. George Cleveland Hall — African American surgeon, CPL board member, and founding member of the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History, who campaigned for a full-service Bronzeville library. Headed by Vivian G. Harsh from 1932 to 1958, it was a leading cultural institution of the Chicago Black Renaissance: birthplace of the 'Special Negro Collection' and home of the Book Review and Lecture Forum (first meeting October 1933). The Harsh collection transferred to the Carter G. Woodson Regional Library in 1975.

name: Grand United Order of Odd Fellows in America
aliases: GUOOF in America; Grand United Order of Odd Fellows
description: Black Odd Fellows order founded 1843 (Philomathean Lodge No. 646, New York City, chartered March 1, 1843 after Peter Ogden's petition to the English Grand United Order of Oddfellows) providing burial, sickness, disability and widowhood benefits through local lodges; its women's auxiliary, the Household of Ruth (founded 1858), gave Black women parallel insurance functions.

name: Griffin Funeral Home
description: Multigenerational Black family funeral business in Bronzeville. Ernest A. Griffin and wife Alyce purchased the Bell Auto and Undertaking Company from his father Stephen A. Griffin in 1947; moved to 3232 S. Martin Luther King Drive in 1969; closed December 31, 2007 after 60 years. Ernest conducted the final rites of Elijah Muhammad and Jesse Owens.

name: Great Northern Realty Company
description: The real-estate / property-holding arm of Anthony Overton's Black business conglomerate in Bronzeville, Chicago (1920s-1940s). Source naming varies between 'Great Northern Realty Company' and 'Northern Realty Company' (see CTL-CFL-002123). It was housed in the Overton Hygienic Building at 3619-3627 S State Street, commissioned by Overton in 1922.

name: Greater Mount Hope Baptist Church
description: Baptist congregation at 6035 Princeton Street, Englewood (presently Mount Hope Baptist Church). Under pastor Rev. William Lambert — a 1962 Chicago delegate to Albany, Georgia, and a Clergy Alliance of Chicago leader in the selective-buying campaign — the church supported the development of Operation Breadbasket and in August 1966 became the South Side Action Center of the Chicago Freedom Movement.

name: Greater Salem Baptist Church
description: Chicago Baptist congregation; Mahalia Jackson's first Chicago church home after her 1927 arrival, and the base of her early choir work and the Johnson Brothers/Johnson Gospel Singers. Within months of arriving, Jackson was the lead vocalist of the 50-member choir and joined the pastor's sons (Prince, Wilbur, and Robert Johnson) and Louise Lemon in the Johnson Singers — described as Chicago's first Black gospel group. The Johnson Brothers were the first organized group to play the Chicago church circuit, staging self-written musical dramas at the church with Jackson in the lead role before splitting in the mid-1930s. The congregation continues today as Greater Salem Missionary Baptist Church on Chicago's South Side.

name: God's Trombones
aliases: God's Trombones: Seven Negro Sermons in Verse
description: Collection of seven sermons in verse by James Weldon Johnson, published in 1927.

description: Downtown Chicago lakefront park (319 acres) that has hosted the Chicago Blues Festival (at the Petrillo Music Shell and festival stages) and the Chicago Gospel Music Festival since the 1980s; the Blues Festival moved to adjacent Millennium Park in 2017.

name: Geneva Smitherman
description: Linguist and educational activist; University Distinguished Professor Emerita at Michigan State University; author of Talkin and Testifyin (1977); scholar of African American Language.

name: General Recorded Tape
description: California tape manufacturer that bought Chess Records from the Chess brothers in 1969 for $6.5 million plus stock; sold the Chess catalog to All Platinum Records in 1975.

name: George E. Johnson
description: Chicago cosmetics entrepreneur (1927-2026) who co-founded Johnson Products Company in 1954 with his wife Joan; creator of Afro Sheen and Ultra Sheen; exclusive sponsor behind Soul Train's national rise.

name: George Jones
description: Brother of Edward 'Big Ed' Jones; ran the Jones brothers' policy enterprise with Edward and Mack in 1930s-40s Bronzeville.

name: George Stauber
description: 24-year-old white man who threw the rocks that struck Eugene Williams at the 29th Street Beach on July 27, 1919; charged with manslaughter but not convicted.

name: Glory Boyz Entertainment
description: Chief Keef’s own label imprint, later developed into Glo Gang.

name: George Jackson Prison Movement
description: Baltimore prison-literacy program founded by W. Paul Coates in 1972; precursor of The Black Book bookstore and Black Classic Press.

name: Good Side, Bad Side
description: Second studio album by Crucial Conflict, released 1998 on Universal Records.

name: Graball Landing (Tallahatchie River), Glendora, Mississippi
description: Riverbank site near Glendora, Mississippi, believed to be where Emmett Till's body was recovered from the Tallahatchie River on August 31, 1955. A memorial sign erected in 2008 was repeatedly vandalized; a one-inch-thick bulletproof sign was dedicated in October 2019. Unit of the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument (established 2023).

name: Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five
description: Hip-hop group founded by Grandmaster Flash in the late 1970s; became the first hip-hop act inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (2007).

name: General Electric
description: General Electric is a major American corporation that appears in the CultureTechLens record as a purchaser of patents from Black inventors. Granville T. Woods, the railway-telegraphy inventor who held dozens of patents, sold patents to General Electric and other major corporations. Garrett Augustus Morgan likewise sold the rights to his three-position traffic signal — U.S. Patent 1,475,024, granted November 20, 1923, whose innovation was a third, all-directional-stop position giving traffic time to clear the intersection — to General Electric for $40,000. The company's documented role in this corpus is thus as the corporate buyer on the other side of two Black inventors' patent sales, in an era when such sales were a principal route by which Black invention entered industrial production.

name: Georgetta Glover
description: Pastor of Greater St. John AME Church, Chicago (6201 S Throop St); preaches the church's Sunday worship series.

name: George H. Miley
description: Nuclear engineer; Professor of Nuclear Engineering at the University of Illinois since 1961; co-inventor with Henry T. Sampson Jr. of the gamma-electric cell (U.S. Patent 3,591,860).

name: Gary, Indiana
description: Indiana city where Capital B opened its second local newsroom in 2023 through the Indiana Local News Initiative with the American Journalism Project.

name: Gender Shades
description: 2018 MIT thesis study by Joy Buolamwini uncovering large racial and gender accuracy disparities in commercial gender-classification AI systems.

name: GTE Government Systems Division
description: GTE division in the Boston/Cambridge area where Kamal Al-Mansour worked after JPL, including on 'Red Ryder,' a U.S. Air Force GPS-technology contract project.

name: Google AI Accra
description: Google's first artificial-intelligence research center in Africa, opened in Accra, Ghana in 2018; headed at launch by Moustapha Cissé.

name: Glen Ford
description: Black journalist; news anchor for the Mutual Black Network.

name: Gordon Bell
description: Pioneer in high-performance and parallel computing; namesake of the Gordon Bell Prize; stated Emeagwali's 1989 prize-winning entry had nothing to do with the internet.

name: Game Changer
description: 'Game Changer: The Technoscientific Revolution in Sports' (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2017) by Rayvon Fouche.

name: Gerhard Sessler
description: German physicist; with James E. West, co-invented the foil electret microphone at Bell Labs (1962); later professor at TU Darmstadt and inventor of the silicon microphone.

name: Greg Perry
description: Songwriter/producer/singer; key player in Holland-Dozier-Holland's Invictus/Hot Wax Records; brother of Jeffree Perry.

name: George W. Ivie
description: Executive director and CEO of the Media Rating Council; announced the reaccreditation of Nielsen's national TV measurement in April 2023 after the 19-month suspension.

name: Georgia Bulldogs football
description: University of Georgia football program (Athens); Mel Tucker was defensive coordinator and defensive backs coach 2016-2018 under head coach Kirby Smart.

name: Gavin Christopher
description: R&B singer, keyboardist, and producer; brother of Shawn Christopher; co-wrote her hit 'Don't Lose the Magic.'

name: Ginger Smock
description: Ginger Smock is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Person (musician), Verified, under project MUSIC-001. Her full name is given as Emma 'Ginger' Smock in the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture's account of pioneering Black women in jazz, 'Women Behind the Music' — the record's sole cited source, and a primary one. She is carried in the African American jazz artists collection as record CTL-JAZZ-017 of the CTL-JAZZ-100 dataset (2026-10-08), where the same Smithsonian-supported claim is the only claim for her and its review status is verified. The graph era is unspecified. No passage in the assigned corpus documents her instrument, dates, recordings, or any Chicago connection, and none is asserted here.

name: George Russell
description: George Russell, cataloged here as a jazz musician, received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1990 — the fact carried by his record's cited source, the consolidated NEA Jazz Masters roster. He is entry CTL-JAZZ-044 in CultureTechLens's CTL-JAZZ-100 dataset of African American jazz artists (2026). The record is the jazz musician of this name, and it should not be confused with the British Formula One driver of the same name: a CTL gap census in October 2026 filed this entity's ID under 'Race Car Drivers,' a misidentification — a driver born in 1998 cannot be a 1990 fellowship recipient — and that categorization should not be relied on. Beyond the fellowship and the cataloging, CTL's corpus holds no further sourced passage about the jazz George Russell.

name: Gerald Wilson
description: Gerald Wilson is a musician recorded in CultureTechLens's African American jazz artists collection (CTL-JAZZ-100 dataset, 2026-10-08), under the alternate identifier CTL-JAZZ-046, as a recipient of the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1990. The record's sole source is the consolidated NEA Jazz Masters roster, adapted from NEA records via Wikipedia. The evidence corpus provided for this tranche contains no further documented biography, era, or Chicago connection for this artist, and the graph era remains unspecified.

name: George Benson
description: George Benson received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 2009, the fact carried by his record's cited source, the consolidated NEA Jazz Masters roster adapted from NEA records. He is cataloged as entry CTL-JAZZ-085 in CultureTechLens's CTL-JAZZ-100 dataset, the project's 2026 collection of one hundred African American jazz artists, where his entry rests on the same roster source. That is the whole of his sourced presence in CTL's corpus: no passage in the research files or project documents read for this fill states his instrument, names a recording, or gives biographical detail, and none is asserted here.

name: GeoCities shutdown
description: GeoCities shutdown is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as an Event (closing), Provisional, under project TECH-001, sourced to the research brief 'Black Chicago Goes Online' (CTL-RB-TECH-000002 v1.0, 2026-10-09). The brief states that Yahoo shut down GeoCities on October 26, 2009, and that the Internet Archive saved what it could find, but had no complete list of pages, so some sites were never collected — the basis for the graph record's summary that preservation was incomplete. The preservation brief adds that Jason Scott led the 2009 Archive Team GeoCities rescue, and that Yahoo deleted whatever owners had not rescued. The brief uses the shutdown as its closing example of what going online left behind. No passage in the corpus documents how much material survived or which communities' pages were lost, and none is asserted here.

name: Genesis Owusu
description: Genesis Owusu (born Kofi Owusu-Ansah on April 17, 1998, in Koforidua, Ghana) is a Ghanaian-Australian rapper and singer based in Canberra, where his family migrated in 2000. His debut album, Smiling with No Teeth (2021) — a genre-blurring confrontation with racism and depression, built with a live band — won four trophies at the 2021 ARIA Music Awards: Album of the Year, Best Hip Hop Release, Best Independent Release and Best Cover Art. The Guardian's reviewer noted the historic frame: he was the first rapper, and only the second person of colour, to take the ARIA Album of the Year title. The follow-up, Struggler (2023), extended his international reach, and his third album, Redstar Wu & the Worldwide Scourge, arrived in 2026.

name: Greensboro Sit-Ins (1960)
description: On February 1, 1960, four freshmen from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College — Ezell Blair Jr., David Richmond, Franklin McCain, and Joseph McNeil — sat down at the segregated lunch counter of the Woolworth's store in Greensboro, North Carolina, asked for coffee, were refused, and stayed until closing. They returned in growing numbers, and within days the sit-in tactic had spread to dozens of Southern cities, carried largely by Black college students who dressed for church, carried their books, and absorbed abuse without returning it. The Greensboro Woolworth's desegregated its counter that July, and the movement the sit-ins ignited produced, in April 1960, a new organization — the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (CTL-E-5421) — founded at Shaw University to coordinate the student wave. The sit-ins mark the moment the freedom movement's center of gravity shifted to the young: students who had not organized Montgomery decided, in a single afternoon, to stop waiting for permission. The intake timeline files this as one stop, 'Sit-In Movement and Founding of SNCC'; the graph holds the event here and the organization beside it.

name: George Floyd Protests (2020)
aliases: George Floyd Protests; Floyd Protests of 2020
description: On May 25, 2020, George Floyd, a forty-six-year-old Black man, was murdered in Minneapolis by police officer Derek Chauvin, who knelt on his neck for more than nine minutes during an arrest over a counterfeit twenty-dollar bill, while a seventeen-year-old bystander's video recorded Floyd's repeated 'I can't breathe.' Protests began in Minneapolis the next day, May 26, and within a week had spread to hundreds of American cities and to capitals around the world, becoming — by the estimates of polls conducted that June — the largest protest movement in United States history, with between fifteen and twenty-six million participants in the United States alone. The protests, conducted in the name and language of Black Lives Matter (CTL-E-5438), demanded accountability for Floyd's killing and reform of American policing; they toppled monuments, rewrote public argument about race in a matter of weeks, and continued through the summer of 2020 and into Chauvin's conviction for murder in April 2021. The intake timeline leaves this stop undated; the audit supplies May 2020. George Floyd himself holds no prior record in the graph and is named here as the event's center.

name: Girlfriends
description: Girlfriends, created by Mara Brock Akil, aired on UPN from September 11, 2000, to May 8, 2006, and on The CW from October 1, 2006, to February 11, 2008 — eight seasons, 172 episodes following Joan Clayton and the three friends whose interior lives, careers, and negotiations with each other were the series' actual subject. Where Living Single had built the form, Girlfriends refined it into a drama of Black women's friendship treated with novelistic patience: the show centered four women's inner lives rather than a romantic pursuit, a framing its cast and creator identify as its breakthrough. It became one of the longest-running Black-led sitcoms of its era, and its ending is part of its history — cancelled in the writers'-strike period without a produced series finale, a loose end its audience has never accepted. It also spun off The Game, extending Akil's television world. The graph files Girlfriends as the 2000s' defining entry in the friendship-sitcom line that runs from Bowser through Akil to Rae — three creators, three decades, one form, all now on the shelf.

name: Godfather of Harlem
description: Godfather of Harlem, created by Chris Brancato and Paul Eckstein with Brancato as showrunner, premiered on Epix on September 29, 2019, and continued on the rebranded MGM+ from its third season in 2023 — four seasons through 2025, with a finale announced after the fourth. Forest Whitaker, also an executive producer, stars as Bumpy Johnson, the Harlem crime boss released from Alcatraz into the 1960s. The series is built as a deliberate collision: Johnson's war with the Genovese family for Harlem's streets runs in the same episodes as his alliance with Malcolm X, played by Nigél Thatch, so that the organized-crime story and the civil-rights movement keep interrupting each other — the show's thesis being that they were never separate stories. Its longevity is itself notable, sustaining a four-season run across a network's rebranding, a migration few premium-cable dramas survive. Industry recognition at check time includes NAACP Image Award nominations for Whitaker's performance in the 2026 cycle and for the fourth season's soundtrack. The graph files it beside the Malcolm X records it dramatizes: history and its underworld, sharing one neighborhood and one decade.

name: Glory (1989 film)
description: Glory, directed by Edward Zwick from Kevin Jarre's screenplay — drawn from Lincoln Kirstein's Lay This Laurel, Peter Burchard's One Gallant Rush, and the letters of Robert Gould Shaw — was released by Tri-Star Pictures in limited release on December 15, 1989, and wide that February 16, 1990. It tells the story of the 54th Massachusetts Infantry, one of the Union Army's earliest Black regiments, from its formation through the assault on Fort Wagner — the same regiment whose war this graph's Civil War record (CTL-E-5409) frames. From five Academy Award nominations it won three, including Best Supporting Actor for Denzel Washington — his first Oscar. In 2025 the Library of Congress selected it for the National Film Registry, thirty-six years after release, the institution's confirmation of the film's standing as the Civil War's defining Black screen narrative. The graph files Glory as the historical-epic shelf's anchor: the film through which most Americans first met the 54th, and the reason the regiment's monument stands in the culture where it does.

name: George Levitan
description: George Levitan was a Fort Worth plumbing merchant, born in Michigan and described in the scholarship as a Jewish American, who in 1950 bought Horace J. Blackwell's magazines and Good Publishing Company and ran them for twenty-six years. Levitan kept the company's Black editorial leadership in place while expanding its line: he renamed The World's Messenger as Bronze Thrills, published the Black-audience magazines Hep and Jive, and renamed Negro Achievements in stages — Sepia Record in 1953, then Sepia in 1954. Under Levitan, Sepia serialized John Howard Griffin's reporting that became Black Like Me and stood for decades as Ebony's most durable competitor. He published Sepia until his death in 1976, when the magazine passed to Beatrice Pringle, a member of Blackwell's founding editorial team. Levitan's personal record in national sources is nearly as thin as Blackwell's; this record is staged Provisional, with its upgrade path named, rather than padded.

name: Good Publishing Company
description: Good Publishing Company (also styled Sepia Publishing) was the Fort Worth, Texas, publishing house behind Sepia and its sister magazines. Founded by clothing merchant Horace J. Blackwell, it issued The World's Messenger from 1942 and Negro Achievements from 1946; an early bibliography lists the magazine's publisher as the Negro Achievements Publishing Company, and the point at which the Good Publishing name attaches is not documented in the sources consulted. Bought by George Levitan in 1950, the company renamed Negro Achievements in stages to Sepia (1954) and The World's Messenger to Bronze Thrills, and also issued Hep and Jive. A May 1975 Fort Worth Star-Telegram photographic record describes the firm producing six magazine covers a month and calls it the only completely self-contained Black magazine publishing firm in the country. Sepia's final issue came in 1983; in 1991 the company's photographic archive was donated to the African American Museum in Dallas. The record is staged Provisional: the operation is documented, the early corporate form is not.

name: Greater Bethesda Missionary Baptist Church
aliases: Greater Bethesda MBC; The Pool of Bethesda; GBMBC
description: Greater Bethesda Missionary Baptist Church is a Washington Park congregation at 109 East 53rd Street, worshiping under the motto "Loving Our God, Living Our Name" and known in its own materials as the Pool of Bethesda. In December 2017 the church marked 135 years of ministry, dating its founding to about 1882. Its longtime pastor Dr. A. Lincoln James Sr., who died on June 28, 2010, at eighty-nine, is remembered as pastor emeritus. The church's current published leadership identifies the Rev. David W. Watkins III — a lifelong member, and by the church's own biography its fifth pastor — as senior pastor, leading a congregation whose ministries address poverty, violence, and education in the Washington Park neighborhood.

name: George Mikan
description: George Lawrence Mikan (June 18, 1924 – June 1, 2005) was basketball's first dominant big man; born in Joliet, Illinois, he is staged here with his center of gravity at DePaul, where his legend was made. A 6-foot-10 Archbishop Quigley Preparatory Seminary student whom coach Ray Meyer rebuilt through coordination work — jump rope, dance lessons, the hook-shot drill that still bears his name — Mikan became a three-time All-American and two-time Helms Foundation Player of the Year (1944, 1945), led the nation in scoring twice, and carried DePaul to the 1945 NIT title with 120 points in three games, including a school-record 53 against Rhode Island that still stands. His shot-swatting forced the NCAA's 1944 goaltending rule. He began his professional career in Chicago with the American Gears of the National Basketball League, winning the 1947 NBL championship, before a dispersal draft sent him to the Minneapolis Lakers, where he won five more championships and was voted by the Associated Press the greatest player of the game's first half-century. He entered the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in its inaugural class of 1959.

name: G Herbo
description: G Herbo, born Herbert Randall Wright III on October 8, 1995, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American rapper from Chicago's South Side. He signs with Machine Entertainment Group at age sixteen in 2011 and first performs as Lil Herb, gaining attention alongside Lil Bibby. His debut mixtape, Welcome to Fazoland, appears in 2014 and is named for his late friend Fazon Robinson. Mixtapes including Pistol P Project, Ballin Like I'm Kobe, and Strictly 4 My Fans follow before his debut studio album, Humble Beast, arrives in 2017. He collaborates with producer Southside on Swervo in 2018 and Still Swervin in 2019. His album PTSD, released in 2020, confronts trauma and mental health and becomes his first top-ten album on the Billboard 200. Later albums include 25 in 2021, Survivor's Remorse in 2022, Big Swerv in 2024, and Lil Herb in 2025. Beyond recording, he launches Swervin' Through Stress, a mental-health initiative providing therapeutic resources for Black young adults in Chicago.

name: Golden State Warriors
aliases: Philadelphia Warriors; San Francisco Warriors; GSW
description: The Golden State Warriors are the NBA franchise founded in 1946 in Philadelphia, where — as the Philadelphia Warriors — they won the Basketball Association of America's first championship in 1947 and a second title in 1956. The franchise moved to the San Francisco Bay Area in 1962, took the name Golden State in 1971, and won the 1975 NBA championship in one of the league's noted Finals upsets. Led by Stephen Curry, Klay Thompson and Draymond Green — a graph record since Wave 3 (CTL-E-5597) — the team won championships in 2015, 2017, 2018 and 2022, set the NBA regular-season record at 73–9 in 2015–16 before losing that year's Finals, and reached five consecutive Finals from 2015 to 2019. The franchise plays at Chase Center in San Francisco, its home since 2019; its seven championships place it among the league's most decorated franchises.

name: George Kirby
description: George Kirby (June 8, 1923 – September 30, 1995) was an American comedian, singer, and actor born in Chicago, Illinois. He broke into show business in the 1940s at the Club DeLisa, the South Side variety house that hired local singers, dancers, and comedians, and made his first recording as a stand-up blues singer, performing “Ice Man Blues” on a 1947 Tom Archia session for Aristocrat Records. Kirby was among the first African-American comedians to appeal to white as well as Black audiences during the Civil Rights era, appearing between 1963 and 1972 on Perry Como's Kraft Music Hall, The Ed Sullivan Show, The Dean Martin Show, The Jackie Gleason Show, Rowan and Martin's Laugh-In, and The Tonight Show. A gifted impressionist, he mimicked white stars such as John Wayne and Walter Brennan — provocative in the 1960s — alongside Bill Cosby and Pearl Bailey, and sang in the voices of Louis Armstrong and Ella Fitzgerald. He produced The George Kirby Show special in 1970 and hosted Half the George Kirby Comedy Hour for 22 episodes in 1972. Kirby died in Las Vegas, Nevada.

name: Giannis Antetokounmpo
aliases: Giannis Sina Ugo Antetokounmpo; Giannis Sina Ugo Adetokunbo; Greek Freak
description: Giannis Antetokounmpo, born Giannis Sina Ugo Adetokunbo on 6 December 1994 in Athens, Greece, is a Greek-Nigerian professional basketball player for the Miami Heat. Born and raised in Athens to Nigerian parents, he played for Filathlitikos before Milwaukee selected him 15th overall in the 2013 NBA draft. Nicknamed the Greek Freak for his size, speed and ball-handling, he won Most Improved Player in 2017, consecutive league Most Valuable Player awards in 2019 and 2020, and Defensive Player of the Year in 2020 — only the third player to win MVP and Defensive Player of the Year in the same season. In 2021 he led Milwaukee to its first championship since 1971 and was unanimous Finals MVP; he left the Bucks as their all-time leader in points, rebounds, assists, blocks, games and minutes, with ten All-Star selections. In June 2026 Milwaukee traded him and Bobby Portis to Miami, and he began the 2026-27 season ranked among the league's top power forwards with the Heat.

name: Gerri Oliver
description: Gerri Oliver — Geraldine “Mama Gerri” Oliver — was the proprietor who made Gerri's Palm Tavern at 446 East 47th Street the premier gathering place of Bronzeville for nearly half a century. A Mississippi native who had worked as a manicurist, she bought the tavern in 1956 from James “Genial Jim” Knight, who had opened it in 1933 and held court as the first “Mayor of Bronzeville.” Under Oliver the Palm Tavern hosted Duke Ellington, Dizzy Gillespie, Billie Holiday, James Brown, Lena Horne, Muddy Waters, and Quincy Jones, and Harold Washington celebrated his 1983 mayoral victory there. The city boarded the building up in an eminent-domain taking in August 2001, and it was later demolished; the tavern itself is homed in the graph at CTL-E-0145. Oliver died on December 7, 2020, at the age of 101, in California. She is a distinct person from Gerri Major, the journalist — the shared first name is a documented collision trap in the sources, and this record is built on the Palm Tavern proprietor only.

name: Gervonta Davis
aliases: Gervonta Bryant Davis; Tank; Tank Davis
description: Gervonta Davis (born in Baltimore, Maryland, in 1994) is an American professional boxer, nicknamed 'Tank,' who has won world championships in three weight divisions and built one of the highest knockout ratios of his era. Raised in West Baltimore, he was for a time the leading name of the Mayweather Promotions stable and won his first world title, at super featherweight, in 2017. He added titles at lightweight and super lightweight, and in April 2023 stopped Ryan Garcia in the seventh round of one of the biggest fights of the decade. On 1 March 2025 at Barclays Center he retained his WBA lightweight title in a majority draw with Lamont Roach Jr., the first blemish on his record, and he has not fought since; in 2026 coverage he was reported as a champion-in-recess while a return was discussed for 2027. Legal record, stated neutrally: Davis pleaded guilty in February 2023 to four counts arising from a November 2020 Baltimore hit-and-run crash and was sentenced in May 2023 to 90 days of home detention, three years of probation and 200 hours of community service; later matters are treated here as procedural only.

name: George Foreman
description: George Foreman (born George Edward Foreman on 10 January 1949 in Marshall, Texas; died 21 March 2025 in Houston, Texas) was an American boxer, minister and entrepreneur who twice held the world heavyweight championship, twenty years apart. Raised in Houston's Fifth Ward, he learned to box in a Job Corps camp and won the heavyweight gold medal at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics. In January 1973 he knocked out the unbeaten Joe Frazier in two rounds in Kingston, Jamaica, to take the title, and he lost it to Muhammad Ali in the eighth round of the 'Rumble in the Jungle' in Kinshasa in October 1974. He retired in 1977, became an ordained minister, and returned a decade later; on 5 November 1994, at 45, he knocked out Michael Moorer to regain the championship, becoming the oldest heavyweight champion in history. He retired for good in 1997 with a record of 76 wins, 68 by knockout, against 5 losses, and reached a second, wider fame as the name behind the George Foreman Grill. His family announced his death, at 76, in March 2025. This record is a tribute.

name: Grambling State University
aliases: Grambling State; GSU; Grambling College; Colored Industrial and Agricultural School; Louisiana Negro Normal and Industrial Institute
description: Grambling State University is a public, historically Black university in Grambling, Louisiana, and a member of the University of Louisiana System. It opened on November 1, 1901, as the Colored Industrial and Agricultural School, founded by the North Louisiana Colored Agricultural Relief Association, a group of Black farmers organized in 1896 who wanted a school for African Americans in the northern part of the state, where almost none existed. At the association's request, Booker T. Washington sent Tuskegee graduate Charles P. Adams, who became the school's founding president and served thirty-five years. The school moved to its present site in 1905, became a state junior college in 1928 as the Louisiana Negro Normal and Industrial Institute, awarded its first baccalaureate degree in 1944, and became Grambling College in 1946. Graduate programs brought university status and the present name in 1974. Grambling's Tigers compete in the Southwestern Athletic Conference, and its football program under coach Eddie G. Robinson, who led the team from 1941 to 1997, made the university nationally known; the campus is listed on the Louisiana African American Heritage Trail.

name: George Clinton
description: George Edward Clinton, born July 22, 1941, in Kannapolis, North Carolina, and raised in Plainfield, New Jersey, is the singer, songwriter, producer, and bandleader who built Parliament-Funkadelic, the defining collective of funk. As a teenager he formed the doo-wop group the Parliaments while working in a Plainfield barbershop, and later worked as a Motown staff songwriter. In the 1970s he directed two bands drawn from one pool of musicians: Parliament, with its horn-driven dance funk and Mothership stage spectacle, and Funkadelic, with its psychedelic guitar rock, together developing P-Funk's mix of Afrofuturist imagery, surreal humor, and dance-floor discipline. He launched a solo career with Computer Games in 1982, home of 'Atomic Dog,' and his catalog became a foundation sample source for hip-hop and G-funk. Clinton was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1997 with fifteen other members of Parliament-Funkadelic, and in 2019 he and the collective received Grammy Lifetime Achievement Awards.

name: George Benton
aliases: George Allen Benton; The Professor; The Mayor of North Philadelphia
description: George Benton, born George Allen Benton on 15 May 1933 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was an American middleweight boxer and one of the most respected trainers in boxing history. Known as the Professor for his scientific, defense-first teaching, he turned professional at sixteen in 1949 and fought until 1970, compiling a record of 61 wins, 13 losses and 1 draw with 36 knockouts, beating future Hall of Famer Joey Giardello in 1962 without ever receiving a world title shot. A shooting in 1970 ended his fighting career. Working under Eddie Futch in Joe Frazier's Philadelphia gym, he was in Frazier's corner for the Thrilla in Manila, then devised the strategy with which Leon Spinks upset Muhammad Ali in 1978. As head trainer with Lou Duva's Main Events he trained champions including Evander Holyfield, Pernell Whitaker, Mike McCallum and Meldrick Taylor, was twice named Trainer of the Year, and entered the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2001. He died in Philadelphia on 19 September 2011, aged seventy-eight.

name: Gary Crusader
description: The Gary Crusader is a Black newspaper based in Gary, Indiana, serving the city of Gary and Northwest Indiana as part of the Crusader Newspaper Group alongside its sister paper, the Chicago Crusader. It was founded in 1961 by Balm L. Leavell Jr. and Joseph H. Jefferson, the founders of the Chicago Crusader in 1940, who established the Gary paper at the invitation of Kelly and Samuel Polk to give a voice to the African American population of Northwest Indiana and to report on the civil rights movement, African American culture and Gary's Black community. It is a distinct publication from the Chicago Crusader, not another name for it. When Balm Leavell died in 1968, his wife Dorothy Leavell took over as editor and publisher of the Gary Crusader, a role Congressional tributes credit with decades of leadership of the Crusader group; she became the second woman to serve as president of the National Newspaper Publishers Association, holding that office from 1995 to 1999, and chaired the NNPA Foundation from 2006 to 2011. The Gary Crusader marked its fifty-fifth anniversary in 2016 and remains a weekly publication and active NNPA member.

name: Georges Collinet
aliases: M'vam Georges Collinet; Maxi Voom Voom
description: Georges Collinet, born in Cameroon to a Cameroonian mother and a French father, is a broadcaster whose French- and English-language programs have linked Africa, Europe, and the United States for six decades. Taken to France for schooling at seven and a half in 1947, he came to the United States at twenty and joined the Voice of America, where his morning program Bonjour l'Afrique made him one of the best-known broadcasters on the African continent. In a 2012 NPR interview he recalled playing James Brown and Wilson Pickett for African listeners despite objections from American embassies, and urging African musicians not to abandon their own traditions and instruments. Working with African musicians in Paris in the 1970s and early 1980s, he supported their efforts to retain African roots while developing a distinctive, professional sound. Since 1988 he has hosted Afropop and Afropop Worldwide, the award-winning public-radio series heard across the United States, Europe, and Africa, and he has also hosted television connecting public-policy and cultural figures across the continent. Afropop Worldwide's own program celebrating him describes a thirty-eight-year hosting career and presents him, in the present tense, as a living legend of African music broadcasting.

name: Gene Demby
description: Gene Demby is an American journalist who serves as co-host and correspondent for Code Switch, NPR's team covering race, ethnicity, and culture. Before coming to NPR, he served as managing editor for HuffPost's BlackVoices vertical following its launch, and later covered politics there. Prior to that role he spent six years in various positions at The New York Times. While working for the Times in 2007, he started PostBourgie, a blog about race, culture, politics, and media, which won the 2009 Black Weblog Award for Best News/Politics Site. Demby is a founding member of the Code Switch team, the NPR project built around fearless conversations about race — how race shapes politics, pop culture, history, food, and everyday life. In 2020 Code Switch was named Apple Podcasts' first-ever Show of the Year. As of NPR's September 2022 announcement, Demby co-hosted the program alongside B.A. Parker, with senior correspondent Karen Grigsby Bates, and journalist Lori Lizarraga announced as a further co-host joining Demby and Parker. NPR Illinois' current people page continues to list Demby as the team's co-host and correspondent, with recent Code Switch episodes carrying his hosting credit.

name: Grace Salome Kwami
aliases: Da Grace; Grace Salome Abra Kwami; Grace Salome Abru Kwami; Grace S. Kwami
description: Grace Salome Kwami (1923–2006), known respectfully as Da Grace, was a Ghanaian sculptor, painter, and art educator and a forerunner of modern art in the colonial Gold Coast, now Ghana. Born Grace Salome Abra Anku into an Ewé Christian family in the Volta Region, she modeled objects in clay from age four and later took the Specialist Art and Crafts course at Achimota College in Accra, which moved in 1952 to the Kumasi College of Technology, excelling in painting and sculpture, specifically portraiture. She was among the first Ghanaian women to receive a formal art education in Ghana. Her figurative portraits — often ordinary people, women, and children — include the oil paintings A Girl in Red (1954) and The Mallam (1954) and terra-cotta portrait heads; around 1960 she made Drum, a large sculpture of a community carrying an oversize drum, which her son Atta Kwami called her most patriotic work. Widowed in 1957, she taught for years, including at Mawuli School and later in Tamale, while keeping a home studio. She cofounded the Sankofa movement for a distinctive Ghanaian modernism, and her work has been reclaimed in recent exhibitions, including African Modernism in America, 1947–67 and the National Museum of Ghana's Ghana 1957: Art After Independence (2024–25).

name: Guion Bluford
aliases: Guion Stewart Bluford Jr.; Guy Bluford; Guion S. Bluford Jr.
description: Guion Stewart Bluford Jr. is an American aerospace engineer, retired Air Force officer and former NASA astronaut, born November 22, 1942, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. He graduated from Overbrook Senior High School in 1960 and earned a bachelor's degree in aerospace engineering from Pennsylvania State University in 1964, followed by master's and doctoral degrees in aerospace engineering from the Air Force Institute of Technology in 1974 and 1978 and an MBA in 1987. As an F-4C fighter pilot he flew 144 combat missions in Southeast Asia, then served as an instructor pilot and in the Air Force Flight Dynamics Laboratory. Selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1978, he launched on August 30, 1983, as a mission specialist on STS-8 aboard Challenger, becoming the first African American to fly in space. He flew three more shuttle missions — STS-61-A in 1985, STS-39 in 1991 and STS-53 in 1992 — logging over 688 hours in space. He retired from NASA and the Air Force in 1993 for aerospace-industry leadership roles, and was inducted into the International Space Hall of Fame in 1997 and the U.S. Astronaut Hall of Fame in 2010.

name: Girls Trip
description: Girls Trip is a 2017 Universal Pictures comedy film directed by Malcolm D. Lee and produced by Will Packer. The R-rated film follows four lifelong friends who reunite for a trip to New Orleans for the annual Essence Festival, where, in Box Office Mojo's synopsis, sisterhoods are rekindled and wild sides rediscovered. Its four leads are Regina Hall, Queen Latifah, Jada Pinkett Smith, and Tiffany Haddish, whose performance, TheWrap wrote, launched her into mainstream stardom. Released on July 21, 2017, the film opened in second place behind Dunkirk and earned a rare A+ CinemaScore from opening-day audiences. Made on a $19 million budget, it became the breakout live-action comedy of its summer: Box Office Mojo's final figures record $115,171,585 in domestic grosses and $140,552,359 worldwide. Its success — a Black women-led ensemble comedy outperforming industry expectations — was widely read in trade coverage as further evidence against the assumption that Black-led films could not travel commercially, and it led to further work between its director, producer, and breakout star at Universal.
